content: To synthesize any human protein, the gene containing the nucleotide sequence that encodes the protein must first be transcribed. For transcription to occur, the RNA polymerase II holoenzyme must locate the gene's promoter. Once the promoter is identified, the transcription start site (TSS) is determined using specific nucleotide sequences that include the TSS. Most human gene promoters lack a TATA box and instead contain an initiator element (Inr) or a downstream promoter element. Various Inr sequences are analyzed to confirm the location of the known TSS. The symbol Inr represents an initiator element, and +1 designates the nucleotide that serves as the TSS. The Inr element in humans was first described and sequenced in 1989. It was found to be more prevalent than the TATA box in eukaryotic core promoter domains, with only 8% of promoters containing a TATA box. Two subunits of the TFIID complex, TAF1 and TAF2, recognize the Inr sequence and facilitate the assembly of the transcriptional machinery. The interaction between TFIID and the Inr sequence is critical for initiating transcription, as the Inr sequence overlaps the TSS. The Inr element also interacts with the transcription factor Sp1 (specificity protein 1), which regulates transcription activation and initiation. Promoters with a functional Inr are less likely to have a TATA box or may contain a degenerate TATA sequence, as the presence of an active Inr reduces dependence on a functional TATA box or additional promoter elements. Although the Inr sequence varies between promoters, it is highly conserved across humans and yeast. An analysis of 7,670 TSSs revealed that approximately 40% matched the BBCA+1BW Inr sequence exactly, while 16% had only one mismatch. TFIID and its subunits are highly sensitive to the Inr sequence, and nucleotide changes can significantly alter binding affinity. The +1 and -3 positions are particularly critical for transcription efficiency and Inr function. For example, replacing the adenosine (A) nucleotide at the +1 position with guanine (G) or thymine (T) reduces transcription activity by 10%, while replacing thymine (T) at the +3 position decreases transcription activity by 22%. Theoretical definitions describe an initiator element as a series of nucleotides, including a TSS, within a gene promoter that triggers a chain reaction or polymerization event, such as transcription. RNA polymerase II can form a stable complex on TATA-less promoters containing Inr elements, which exhibit a weak intrinsic preference for Inr-like sequences. The BRCA1 gene encodes a nuclear phosphoprotein involved in maintaining genomic stability and acts as a tumor suppressor. The BRCA1 protein forms a large multi-subunit complex known as the BRCA1-associated genome surveillance complex (BASC) by interacting with other tumor suppressors, DNA damage sensors, and signal transducers. It also associates with RNA polymerase II and interacts with histone deacetylase complexes via its C-terminal domain. BRCA1 plays roles in transcription, DNA repair of double-stranded breaks, and recombination. Mutations in BRCA1 account for approximately 40% of inherited breast cancers and over 80% of inherited breast and ovarian cancers. Alternative splicing modulates the subcellular localization and physiological function of BRCA1, with many splice variants described, some of which are associated with disease. A related pseudogene is located on chromosome 17. The DHX9 gene encodes an enzyme that catalyzes the ATP-dependent unwinding of double-stranded RNA and DNA-RNA complexes. This protein, a member of the DEAH-box RNA helicase family, localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm and functions as a transcriptional regulator. It may also be involved in the expression and nuclear export of retroviral RNAs. Alternative splicing results in multiple transcript variants, and pseudogenes are found on chromosomes 11 and 13. Overexpression of a fragment of RNA helicase A (RHA) inhibits endogenous BRCA1 function, leading to defects in ploidy and cytokinesis in mammary epithelial cells. RHA links the BRCA1 protein to the RNA polymerase II holoenzyme complex. The CTDP1 gene encodes a protein that interacts with the carboxy-terminus of the RAP74 subunit of transcription initiation factor TFIIF. It functions as a phosphatase that dephosphorylates the C-terminal domain of POLR2A (a subunit of RNA polymerase II), making it available for gene expression initiation. Mutations in CTDP1 are associated with congenital cataracts, facial dysmorphism, and neuropathy syndrome (CCFDN). Alternative splicing produces different isoforms of this protein. The DDX53 gene encodes a protein with domains characteristic of the DEAD-box helicase family, which participates in ATP-dependent RNA unwinding. DEAD/DEAH-box helicases are implicated in various cellular processes involving RNA secondary structure alterations, such as translation initiation, splicing, and ribosome assembly. Some members of this family are involved in embryogenesis, spermatogenesis, and cellular growth and division. The DDX53 protein may play a role in melting DNA:RNA hybrids during transcription and in X-linked gene expression. It contains RNA-binding domains and an RGG box, which regulate RNA helicase activity. In genes lacking a TATA box, the Inr serves as a functional analog, directing transcription initiation with a consensus sequence of 5'-YYA+1NWYY-3'. TATA-less core promoters that do not stably bind TBP (TATA-binding protein) may assemble pre-initiation complexes (PICs) via alternative pathways and are regulated by distinct mechanisms. The Inr facilitates the binding of transcription factor TFIID, which includes TAF1 and TAF2 subunits. These subunits bind to core promoter sequences encompassing the TSS and interact with activators and other transcriptional regulators, influencing the rate of transcription initiation. The Inr is the only known functional analog of the TATA box in metazoan protein-coding genes, sufficient for directing accurate transcription initiation in TATA-less genes. General transcription factor IIA (TFIIA) is critical for the cooperative binding of TFIID to the Inr. TFIID is the first protein to bind DNA during the formation of the RNA polymerase II pre-initiation complex. General transcription factor IIB (TFIIB) and TFIIF also play roles in transcription initiation. The Inr typically contains the TSS and is recognized by TAF1 and TAF2 of the TFIID complex. Transcription does not necessarily begin at the +1 nucleotide for the Inr to function, as RNA polymerase II can be redirected to alternative start sites under specific conditions. Hypotheses suggest that the A1BG gene is not transcribed by an initiator element or a TATA box.
